with: cashew paste, or ash-gourd / bottle-gourd paste, or hung curd
rationale: Achieves the same silky richness with far less saturated fat. Ash gourd is described in the texts as nourishing and cooling.
ayurvedic_basis: Kushmanda (ash gourd): nourishing, cold, alleviates pitta.

with: jaggery (guda) or unheated honey
rationale: Unrefined sweeteners retain minerals and were the standard sweeteners in historical Indian cooking.
ayurvedic_basis: Guda (jaggery) is used throughout classical dietetics; honey should not be heated.

with: whole wheat (godhuma) or millets (bajra, ragi, jowar)
rationale: Whole grains add fibre and were the grains actually used; the Manasollasa flatbreads use whole wheat.
ayurvedic_basis: Godhuma (wheat) is the base of Mandaka, Polika and Purika in the Manasollasa.

with: steaming (svinna / putapaka) or roasting on a low fire
rationale: The texts repeatedly steam, bake or roast vegetables rather than deep-fry them, cutting fat.
ayurvedic_basis: Putapaka (baking in leaves) and svinna (steaming) appear across the Kshemakutuhalam vegetable methods.

with: rock salt (saindhava)
rationale: Rock salt is the salt named in nearly every historical recipe and is considered the most balanced in Ayurveda.
ayurvedic_basis: Saindhava lavana is the preferred salt in classical dietetics.

with: roasted rice powder or gram flour (besan)
rationale: Traditional thickeners used in the texts, e.g. roasted rice powder with coconut, or gram flour in flower-vegetable gravies.
ayurvedic_basis: Roasted rice powder thickens the Kshemakutuhalam brinjal-with-coconut dish; gram flour thickens the hibiscus preparation.

with: buttermilk (takra) simmered with gram flour and spices
rationale: A light, tangy gravy base used historically instead of cream — as in the hibiscus and fish preparations.
ayurvedic_basis: Takra (buttermilk) is prized as light and digestive; used as the cooking medium across many recipes.

with: tamarind or kokum (vriksamla) and sour buttermilk
rationale: Historical souring agents; tomato is a post-Columbian introduction and absent from ancient texts.
ayurvedic_basis: Vriksamla (Malabar tamarind / kokum) is the souring agent in the Manasollasa fish recipe.

with: elephant-foot yam (surana) or colocasia / other traditional tubers
rationale: Traditional starchy tubers used before the potato reached India; documented with cooking methods.
ayurvedic_basis: Surana stimulates digestion, is light; cures piles and cough.

with: black pepper (maricha) and long pepper (pippali)
rationale: Chilli is post-Columbian; the pungent heat in ancient recipes came from pepper. Gentler on the stomach for many.
ayurvedic_basis: Maricha (black pepper) is the near-universal pungent spice across the texts.

with: hand-pounded or red / brown rice
rationale: Less-processed rice keeps more fibre and nutrients; closer to historically milled rice.
ayurvedic_basis: Rice (tandula/odana) is central to the diet; minimal processing preferred.

with: cold-pressed sesame oil (tila taila), mustard oil, or ghee in moderation
rationale: The fats actually used in the texts; sesame and mustard oils and modest ghee, not industrial oils.
ayurvedic_basis: Tila taila (sesame oil) and ghrita (ghee) are the standard cooking fats in the classical recipes.

with: slow-reduced low-fat milk (rabri-style) sweetened lightly with jaggery
rationale: Reduced milk gives the same richness in sweets without the concentrated refined sugar of tinned condensed milk.
ayurvedic_basis: Milk reductions (kshira-paka) are the classical base for sweets like payasa.

with: thickened low-fat milk or fresh paneer
rationale: Lighter dairy keeps the body of the sweet with less fat.
ayurvedic_basis: Fresh curdled and reduced milk are traditional; lighter than full-fat khoya.

with: fresh low-fat paneer or hung curd
rationale: Fresh paneer or hung curd gives the dairy note without emulsifiers or excess salt.
ayurvedic_basis: Fresh curdled milk (paneer-type) is the traditional soft cheese.

with: natural fermentation with curd or a ground urad-dal batter
rationale: Traditional fluffiness came from fermentation, not chemical leaveners.
ayurvedic_basis: Fermented urad-dal/rice batter (iddarika) is the historical leavening method in the Manasollasa.

with: natural colour: turmeric (yellow), saffron (orange), beetroot (red), spinach (green)
rationale: Natural pigments colour the dish without synthetic dyes.
ayurvedic_basis: Turmeric and saffron are traditional colouring-and-medicinal spices.

with: whole-wheat or millet flatbread / bun
rationale: Whole-grain breads add fibre; white bread is a modern refined-flour product.
ayurvedic_basis: Whole wheat (godhuma) is the historical bread grain (Mandaka, Polika).

with: hung-curd dressing with roasted cumin and black salt
rationale: Hung curd gives a creamy dressing without the egg-and-oil fat load.
ayurvedic_basis: Curd-based dressings (raita) are the traditional cool, creamy accompaniment.

with: whole-wheat or millet pasta, or sevai (whole-grain vermicelli)
rationale: Whole-grain versions add fibre and a lower glycaemic load.
ayurvedic_basis: Whole grains and millets are the traditional cereal staples.

with: roasted onion-tomato base, asafoetida and amchur for savoury depth
rationale: Builds umami from whole ingredients instead of an additive.
ayurvedic_basis: Asafoetida (hing) and roasted aromatics are the traditional flavour boosters.

with: a small amount of jaggery, honey or date paste
rationale: Whole-food sweeteners in moderation instead of synthetic ones.
ayurvedic_basis: Jaggery and honey are the classical sweeteners.

with: ghee in moderation or cold-pressed oil
rationale: Avoids trans-fat-prone hydrogenated spreads.
ayurvedic_basis: Ghee (ghrita) is the valued traditional fat, used sparingly.

with: jaggery or date syrup; hung-curd (shrikhand-style) topping
rationale: Unrefined sweetness and a curd-based topping instead of refined-sugar frosting.
ayurvedic_basis: Hung curd (shrikhand) and jaggery are traditional sweet finishes.

with: fresh lean protein (chicken, fish) or legumes and paneer
rationale: Fresh protein avoids the salt, nitrates and saturated fat of cured meats.
ayurvedic_basis: Freshly cooked meats and legumes are used in the texts; nothing cured/preserved.

with: whole fresh fruit, or nimbu pani sweetened with jaggery
rationale: Whole fruit keeps the fibre and skips added sugar and preservatives.
ayurvedic_basis: Fresh fruit and lightly sweetened waters are the traditional refreshments.

with: dark cacao with jaggery, or a nut-and-date paste
rationale: Less sugar and milk solids; more actual cacao.
ayurvedic_basis: Nut-and-date sweets are the traditional rich-sweet analogue.

with: freshly ground spices and freshly made batters
rationale: Fresh preparation avoids preservatives, excess salt and refined fillers.
ayurvedic_basis: Stone-ground fresh spice blends are the historical norm.

with: cold-pressed groundnut, sesame or mustard oil
rationale: Traditional cold-pressed oils in place of industrial palm/hydrogenated fats.
ayurvedic_basis: Sesame (tila) and mustard oils are the classical cooking oils.

with: light coconut milk or a coconut-buttermilk blend
rationale: Lighter coconut base keeps the flavour with less saturated fat.
ayurvedic_basis: Coconut is used moderately in coastal cooking.

with: jaggery syrup or date syrup
rationale: Whole-food syrups replace refined glucose.
ayurvedic_basis: Jaggery is the classical liquid sweetener base.

with: agar-agar (china grass)
rationale: A plant setting agent replaces animal gelatin.
ayurvedic_basis: China grass (agar) is the traditional vegetarian setting agent for sweets.

with: thickened milk with cardamom and saffron
rationale: Real reduced milk and spices instead of coloured cornflour powder.
ayurvedic_basis: Spiced milk reductions are the classical dessert base.

with: plain rolled oats or millets with fresh fruit
rationale: Skips the added sugar and flavourings of instant sachets.
ayurvedic_basis: Whole grains with fruit are the traditional light meal.

with: use sparingly; build savour with roasted aromatics, amchur and tamarind
rationale: Cuts sodium and additives while keeping umami depth.
ayurvedic_basis: Roasted aromatics and sour agents give savour traditionally.

with: lemon juice, kokum or tamarind
rationale: Natural souring agents in place of synthetic vinegar.
ayurvedic_basis: Kokum, tamarind and lemon are the classical souring agents.

with: fresh tomato-tamarind or date chutney
rationale: Fresh chutney avoids the added sugar and preservatives of bottled sauces.
ayurvedic_basis: Fresh ground chutneys are the traditional condiment.

with: plain curd with fresh fruit and a little jaggery
rationale: Plain curd with fruit skips the added sugar of flavoured pots.
ayurvedic_basis: Fresh curd (dadhi) is a classical staple.

with: toned / low-fat milk
rationale: Lower-fat milk where the recipe doesn't need the extra cream.
ayurvedic_basis: Milk is valued; the fat content is adjusted to the person.

with: whole-grain jaggery cookies or roasted snacks
rationale: Whole grains and jaggery instead of maida and refined sugar.
ayurvedic_basis: Roasted grain-and-jaggery snacks are the traditional teatime food.

with: roasted makhana, chana or nuts
rationale: Roasted snacks give crunch without deep-frying or preservatives.
ayurvedic_basis: Roasted grains and fox-nuts are traditional dry snacks.

with: semolina, besan or crushed poha coating
rationale: Whole-grain coatings replace refined breadcrumbs.
ayurvedic_basis: Semolina and gram flour are traditional coatings.

with: coconut water, buttermilk or a herbal kadha
rationale: Natural hydrating drinks instead of caffeine-and-sugar loads.
ayurvedic_basis: Buttermilk and coconut water are classical restoratives.

with: chilled hung curd or a little fresh malai
rationale: Real dairy in small amounts instead of hydrogenated toppings.
ayurvedic_basis: Fresh cream (malai) used sparingly is traditional.
